Patches to the vendored tailscale-rs crates
===========================================

What is here
------------
The folders here -- tailscale, ts_runtime, ts_control, ts_netstack_smoltcp, ts_derp and
ts_netmon -- are copies of the tailscale-rs crates of the same names, version 0.7.1 from
crates.io, with ThinkTerm's changes on top. The root Cargo.toml points crates.io's versions at
them ([patch.crates-io]) and keeps them out of the workspace (exclude). Every other
tailscale-rs crate (ts_keys, ts_tunnel, ...) still comes from crates.io, held at the same
version by Cargo.lock.

Only thinkterm-tailnet-engine/src/node.rs calls the library; the rest of ThinkTerm goes
through it: thinkterm-tailnet on a desktop or a server, thinkterm-mobile on a phone.

Finding our changes
-------------------
Every change is marked with a comment starting "ThinkTerm (<group>)", one of the groups
below:

    grep -rn "ThinkTerm (" deps/tailscale-rs --exclude=PATCHES.txt

The whole difference from upstream, at any time, against a fresh copy of 0.7.1:

    for c in tailscale ts_runtime ts_control ts_netstack_smoltcp ts_derp ts_netmon; do
        curl -sL "https://static.crates.io/crates/$c/$c-0.7.1.crate" | tar xz -C /tmp
        diff -ru "/tmp/$c-0.7.1" "deps/tailscale-rs/$c"
    done

Upstream files this copy does not carry (README.md, examples, tests, benches, Cargo.lock,
Cargo.toml.orig, .cargo_vcs_info.json, and the rest of the repository the tailscale crate
ships) show up as "Only in", and so do the LICENSE and PATENTS that ts_runtime, ts_control,
ts_netstack_smoltcp, ts_derp and ts_netmon got from the tailscale crate, as they ship
without them. All of that is expected.

The changes
-----------
ios (ts_netmon)
    The network monitor's macOS code is for every Apple system: each `target_os = "macos"`
    in the crate's sources and its Cargo.toml is `target_vendor = "apple"`, and nothing
    else is changed. iOS has the same route socket and sysctl dumps; upstream has a monitor
    for macOS, Linux and Windows only, so the library does not build for a phone.
    Redoing it on a new version, from a fresh copy of the crate:
        grep -rl 'target_os = "macos"' src Cargo.toml | xargs perl -pi -e \
            's/target_os = "macos"/target_vendor = "apple"/g'
    Used by: the phone app, which holds a node of its own (thinkterm-mobile's tailnet.rs).
    Drop when: upstream's monitor builds for iOS.

older tokio (ts_netmon)
    The route socket is registered with tokio's AsyncFd::new, as 0.6.1 did. 0.7.1 calls
    AsyncFd::register, which tokio has from 1.53.3 on, while its Cargo.toml asks for any
    tokio 1; the workspace's tokio (Cargo.lock) is older, and macOS and iOS did not build.
    Only Apple systems compile this code, so a Linux build does not show it; see Upgrading.
    Drop when: the workspace's tokio is 1.53.3 or newer.

peer list (tailscale, ts_runtime)
    Device::peers lists every peer in the tailnet; upstream only looks one up by name or
    address. The peer tracker also answers at once when a netmap shows the tailnet has no
    other peers, instead of leaving the question waiting.
    Used by: the Tailscale group on the Remote Hosts page.
    Drop when: upstream can list all peers without waiting.

device info (ts_control; struct literals in ts_runtime's peer_db tests)
    Node keeps, as DeviceInfo, the system, distribution and device model a peer reports in
    its Hostinfo; upstream drops them.
    Used by: the machine icons and subtitles on the Remote Hosts page.
    Drop when: upstream keeps this on Node.

sign-in state (tailscale, ts_runtime)
    Device::current_auth_state, current_self_node and registration_error answer at once with
    where signing in stands; upstream's questions wait until it is done. When a registration
    fails, the control runner stays in a Failed state that says why, instead of stopping
    with the reason only in the log. A machine control knows and has not let in -- one
    waiting for an admin's approval, as a rule, or one whose auth key is wrong -- is
    upstream's own AuthKeyRejected state (since 0.7.0, which answers AuthUrl with it); what
    registration_error says of it is a constant (ts_runtime's control_runner::NOT_LET_IN,
    tailscale::REGISTRATION_NOT_LET_IN), so that whoever shows the device can tell that wait
    from an error. Upstream's docs of the state call it final; notes beside them say that
    the runner asks again (sign-in retry), and the machine may still get in.
    Used by: the Tailscale panel's status, login link and error message.
    Drop when: upstream offers status queries that do not wait, and keeps the reason a
    registration failed.

sign-in retry (ts_runtime)
    A registration that fails is asked again after a while, as tailscaled does, instead of
    the control runner staying failed until the device is made anew: a sign-in follow-up
    whose long poll was cut (the network, an app put away while its user signs in) is asked
    again with the same address, and anew after two cuts in a row; a device control has not
    let in asks again every 10 seconds, so it gets in soon after an admin approves it; any
    other failure after 2 seconds, doubling up to 30. A try after a network or HTTP failure
    goes on a new connection from the dialer.
    Used by: thinkterm-tailnet-engine (a node waiting for approval is not stuck; a failed
    sign-in shows as still connecting).
    Drop when: upstream retries registration by itself.

shutdown (tailscale)
    Device::stop stops a device that is still shared: gracefully within a timeout, else
    violently.
    Used by: thinkterm-tailnet when it ends or replaces its node.
    Drop when: upstream's shutdown works on a shared device.

no panic (ts_runtime)
    kameo 0.21 panics in Context::forward and try_forward when the target's mailbox is full
    or closed. The registry and Env::forward ask from a task instead, so those cases come
    back as errors. Env::ask backs off from 10 ms to 1 s when it retries an actor that has
    stopped, instead of spinning; its Cargo.toml gains tokio's "time" feature for that.
    Drop when: upstream moves to a kameo without the panic, or stops forwarding this way.

lost peers (ts_netstack_smoltcp)
    TCP sockets get a 10-minute timeout and a 2-minute keep-alive, so a peer that disappears
    without a word (a laptop put to sleep) ends the connection instead of leaving it
    retrying forever. The change is in the crate's netcore module, which was the
    ts_netstack_smoltcp_core crate up to 0.6.1.
    Drop when: upstream sets a timeout and a keep-alive on its sockets.

direct fallback (ts_runtime)
    A peer's direct path that stops answering is given up: once two probing rounds of
    path_discoverer's PeerPd in a row had no path answer (UNANSWERED_ROUNDS_BEFORE_DERP), it
    publishes None, once for the streak, which puts the peer back on DERP. A round that
    cannot probe at all -- the peer's disco key or coordinator endpoints unknown, this node
    with no endpoint to offer -- counts as one without an answer. Upstream publishes only a
    round with an answer (its `latencies_was_empty` is read after the map is cleared, so it
    is always true), and traffic stayed on a direct path that had stopped answering -- a
    phone gone from Wi-Fi to cellular, a laptop that changed networks -- until another path
    answered. A round is PROBE_PERIOD, 5 s, with one ping per path: two rounds, so that a
    ping or a pong lost does not send traffic over DERP for a round (nor, with the peer's
    DERP region down, nowhere), and traffic is back on DERP 10 to 15 s after its path stops
    answering.
    Used by: every connection over the tailnet, now that nodes find direct paths: since
    0.7.0 a node sends STUN from its own UDP socket and offers the address it learns
    (tailscale-rs #434), where 0.6.1 never did, so only peers on the same network went
    direct.
    Drop when: upstream withdraws a direct path that stops answering.

stun probes (ts_runtime)
    A STUN probe ends with the future that waits for it (stunner's EndProbe): it is stopped,
    and its subscription to the bus's IncomingStunMsg taken off. In 0.7.1 a probe only
    stopped when its own answer came; dropping its ActorRef when try_stun gave up on it was
    meant to end it, but the bus holds a strong Recipient of it too. So a probe nothing
    answered lived as long as the node -- one more about every 3 s while UDP is blocked, each
    handed every STUN answer after -- and one whose DirectActor was gone waited for it
    without end.
    Drop when: upstream ends a STUN probe it gave up on.

map update (ts_runtime)
    An update of the map request -- this node's endpoints or DERP latencies changed -- that
    fails is logged, and one that takes over 15 s given up; the next map request carries
    them. 0.7.1 unwraps it, so a failure panicked the control runner, and with it every
    question ThinkTerm asks the node, which then made the node anew, dropping every
    connection; and it waits without a limit, the runner answering nothing else meanwhile.
    Since 0.7.0 the address STUN finds is one of the endpoints, and it changes with the
    network, just as the connection to control goes down.
    Drop when: upstream's control runner takes a failed map update in its stride.

refused sends (ts_runtime)
    DirectActor's UDP receive goes on past ConnectionReset. Windows reports an ICMP port
    unreachable for something the socket sent -- a STUN server, a peer's address that is
    gone -- as WSAECONNRESET from the next receive; the socket is fine. As an error it ended
    the receive stream, and DirectActor panicked and was made anew on new ports. Since 0.7.0
    the socket also sends STUN to every DERP region's server. Other systems do not report
    these on a socket that is not connected.
    Drop when: upstream turns SIO_UDP_CONNRESET off or skips the error.

derp dial (ts_derp, ts_runtime)
    A DERP region whose servers cannot be reached, or whose TLS handshake fails, is an error
    for its client; 0.6.1 unwraps the outcome of the dial and panics. A connection gets 15 s
    to come up, as none of its steps has a limit of its own. After a failure the region's
    runner waits and tries again, from 1 s doubling to 30 s, starting from 1 s again once a
    connection held for 10 s. While it waits, what is queued for the region is dropped as it
    comes, and the region becoming home ends the wait. 0.6.1's runner returned on any error,
    leaving the region without a client. A try after a failed one starts with the region's
    next server: the dial goes down a region's servers only up to the first that takes the
    TCP connection, so one that then failed the TLS handshake, or said nothing till the 15 s
    ran out, kept the others from ever being tried.
    Drop when: upstream's DERP client reports a failed dial and its runner retries.

derp frames (ts_derp)
    A frame from a DERP server too short for its type -- a PeerGone without its reason byte,
    as servers from before the reason send, or a packet without its source key -- is passed
    over, and an unknown PeerGone reason only logged; 0.6.1 unwraps the first two, panicking,
    and ends the connection over the third.
    Drop when: upstream's client takes such frames in its stride.

derp reads (ts_derp)
    A DERP connection that has gone 120 s without a frame from the server counts as gone: the
    server sends a keep-alive whenever it has had nothing else to send for a minute, and Go's
    client allows as long. 0.6.1 waited for good, so a connection that died while nothing was
    sent on it -- the machine slept, the network changed -- held its runner, often the home
    region's, and the node got nothing more through it. Its Cargo.toml gains tokio's "time"
    feature for that, and "io-util", as its tests run over tokio::io::duplex.
    Drop when: upstream's client times its reads out.

derp runner (ts_runtime)
    A region's runner ends with its Uniderp: Uniderp::on_stop stops it, and the runner leaves
    by itself once the Uniderp's end of the home-derp watch is gone. kameo leaves a linked task
    running when a supervised actor is restarted, stops normally or goes down with its
    supervisor, and 0.6.1's runner then spun at full speed on the closed watch for as long as
    the process lived. The runner also ends when the dataplane closes its queue, which 0.6.1
    took for activity and connected over, again and again with no wait. A runner ending while
    its Uniderp lives fails the Uniderp, which is restarted with a new transport; by kameo's
    default the Uniderp stayed up with no runner, and the region had no client.
    A Uniderp that stops leaves its queue to a task that empties it until the dataplane goes:
    routes lead to the transport until they are redone, and the dataplane unwraps each send,
    so a packet coming meanwhile panicked it and it restarted empty. A Uniderp kameo restarts
    asks the bus for the latest DERP latency measurement (RetainedBus's GetRetained::new):
    keeping its actor id, it is not sent what the bus retains, and a restarted home region
    took itself for any other until the DERP map changed.
    Drop when: upstream ties the runner's lifetime to its Uniderp's.

derp regions (ts_runtime)
    A region whose Uniderp failed too often to be restarted is given up on its own, and
    started once more a minute later if the DERP map still has it; by kameo's default
    Multiderp stopped with it, and every other region's client went down too. Given up again
    within 30 minutes of that, it waits twice as long each time, up to 30 minutes, as every
    start takes a transport the dataplane keeps for good; DERP maps that come meanwhile do not
    start it early. A Uniderp whose region left the DERP map stops normally and is not
    restarted (0.6.1 restarted it five times, each taking a transport); should the map have
    the region again by the time it is gone, it is started again at once.
    Multiderp keeps its own record of each region's Uniderp, from its spawn until it is gone
    for good, instead of looking it up in the registry: a Uniderp is there only once started,
    so a map coming meanwhile started a second one for the region, and one gone for good
    keeps its name there, so its region never came back. Multiderp also takes the region's
    transport out of its map itself once the Uniderp is gone for good. Uniderp::on_stop did,
    but kameo tells the supervisor before it runs on_stop: the Uniderp restarted in its place
    could put its transport in first, and out it went.
    Drop when: upstream's Multiderp outlives a region it gave up and starts it again.

build (all six)
    #![doc = include_str!("../README.md")] became a one-line //! doc in the lib.rs of
    ts_runtime, ts_control, ts_derp, ts_netmon and ts_netstack_smoltcp, and so did
    include_str!("README.md") in ts_netstack_smoltcp's netcore/mod.rs and netsock/mod.rs: the
    READMEs are not vendored (the root .gitignore drops *.md). In Cargo.toml, tailscale loses
    its [[example]], [[test]] and [profile.*] sections, ts_netmon its [[example]] and [[test]]
    sections, ts_derp its [[example]] sections, and ts_netstack_smoltcp its [[example]],
    [[test]] and [[bench]] sections and its [dev-dependencies] (cargo will not test a crate
    outside the workspace that has any): the vendored copy carries no examples, tests or
    benches. Upstream's proptest module in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/peer_db.rs is switched
    off, as proptest is not a dependency here.

Gone
----
android (ts_netmon), until 0.6.1
    PlatformMon was re-exported everywhere, so the crate did not build for Android, which
    Rust counts as a system of its own rather than Linux. 0.7.0 re-exports it only where the
    crate has one (tailscale-rs #467). On Android platform_mon() is None and the runtime runs
    without a monitor: no local-network endpoints are offered and a change of network is not
    seen; the phone app makes its node anew when the network changes (thinkterm-mobile's
    tailnet::restart). The address STUN finds is the node's endpoint for direct paths there.
    The Linux monitor is not to be borrowed for Android: it binds NETLINK_ROUTE, which apps
    targeting Android 11 and up may not.

Tests
-----
The additions above are called from thinkterm-tailnet, so losing one in a merge fails the
build. The changes in behaviour have tests:

    cargo test -p ts_runtime -p ts_control -p ts_netstack_smoltcp -p ts_derp --lib

    lost peers      netcore::socket_impl::tcp::tests (connect and listen)
    device info     node::tests
    sign-in state   control_runner::tests (the reason given, a machine not let in)
    no panic        env::tests
    direct fallback path_discoverer::tests (a direct path that stops answering, one that
                    misses a round, rounds that cannot probe)
    stun probes     stunner::tests (probes nothing answers)
    derp dial       multiderp::uniderp::tests (an unreachable region, becoming home, a
                    connection that does not come up, the next server)
    derp reads      client::tests in ts_derp (a connection gone quiet, keep-alives)
    derp runner     multiderp::uniderp::tests (a runner whose Uniderp is gone, whose queue
                    is closed, that ended; a region given up; the transport of a Uniderp
                    gone; a Uniderp restarted in the home region)
    derp regions    multiderp::tests (the waits); multiderp::uniderp::tests (a region given
                    up, waiting out its wait, getting one Uniderp, dropped from the map and
                    put back)

Not covered by a test: the peer tracker's answer for an empty tailnet, and the Failed state
taking the place of the stop. Signing in to a real tailnet after an upgrade checks the
first; signing in while the control server cannot be reached checks the second. Nor are the
parts of derp dial and derp frames that need a working DERP server (the waits starting over
after a connection that held, frames the server sends). Map update needs a control server:
changing networks under a signed-in node checks it. Refused sends happen on Windows only: a
node there with a DERP region's STUN server unreachable checks them.

Upgrading
---------
1. Read upstream's CHANGELOG.md for the new version: its security fixes, and anything that
   touches the groups above. A group upstream now covers can be dropped instead of merged.
   A crate upstream no longer publishes under its name (0.7.0 made ts_netstack_smoltcp_core
   the netcore module of ts_netstack_smoltcp) is moved by hand first: vendor the crate that
   holds it now, carry our changes over, and update [patch.crates-io].
2. For each crate here, merge three ways, file by file: the base is upstream's old version,
   ours is deps/tailscale-rs/<crate>, theirs is upstream's new version. With both versions
   unpacked in /tmp as above:

       git merge-file deps/tailscale-rs/<crate>/src/<file> /tmp/<crate>-<old>/src/<file> \
           /tmp/<crate>-<new>/src/<file>

   Changes that do not overlap merge by themselves; overlapping ones are left between
   conflict markers. Copy files upstream added; move by hand our changes in a file upstream
   removed or renamed. Cargo.toml merges the same way; check that no section the build group
   removes came back. Then make every `target_os = "macos"` left in ts_netmon, new ones
   included, `target_vendor = "apple"` (ios), and every README include a one-line doc (build).
3. Bump the version: the six entries under [patch.crates-io] in the root Cargo.toml and the
   two in thinkterm-tailnet-engine/Cargo.toml. The next cargo command (`cargo metadata
   --format-version 1 >/dev/null` will do) brings the other tailscale-rs crates in
   Cargo.lock to the same version; all tailscale-rs crates move together. Check that nothing
   else in Cargo.lock moved but what the new crates need.
4. Build, run the tests above and thinkterm-tailnet's, thinkterm-tailnet-engine's (with
   --features node) and thinkterm-tailnet-node's (with -- --test-threads=1: thinkterm-tailnet's
   keeper tests write a script and run it at once, and race each other in parallel). Check the systems a Linux build does not
   compile: Android (`cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a check -p thinkterm-mobile --lib`), Windows
   (`cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu -p thinkterm-tailnet -p
   thinkterm-tailnet-node`), and Apple's network monitor, which builds without the Apple SDK
   (`cargo check -p ts_netmon --target aarch64-apple-ios`, then aarch64-apple-darwin;
   `rustup target add` them first). Then sign in to a real tailnet and connect to a machine
   by name and by address.
5. Update this file: the version above, and every group that changed or went away.
